The B73 checks at the production run’s sites

Read counts of the 23 B73 checks at the variant-calling production run’s union sites (run 1367152, chr1-chr10; 2026-10-17)

Author

Fausto Rodríguez-Zapata

Published

October 17, 2026

Why

CRISP is meant to run on three kinds of pool per donor: its BC1 pools, the in silico pool of its NILs, and a pool of the B73 checks that are not contaminated (user, 2026-10-17). A donor’s own pools share almost all its variants, so the B73 checks give CRISP its contrast. This notebook asks which B73 checks are clean, using only the production run’s calls: every union site of run 1367152 (chr1-chr10), and each check’s reads there.

  • ALT reads: reads carrying the run’s ALT allele at a site; other reads: a third allele; ALT share = ALT reads / all reads at the run’s sites.
  • The checks: the 12 batch-1 B73-bulk checks (the pipeline’s check filter tests these) and the 11 batch-2 B73 checks (in the run’s sheet, never tested or used).
  • Reads are counted as the run counts the BC1 pools at the union: MAPQ and base quality >= 20, no duplicate, secondary or supplementary records.

The two batches

Mismatches over the whole genome

samtools stats of each check’s CRAM (alignment QC): mismatches over all mapped bases, no site list. In B73 nearly every mismatch is a sequencing error, so this ranks the checks by sequencing quality; contamination adds little to it (5 % teosinte reads, which differ from B73 at ~1 % of their bases, add ~0.05 %).

Along the genome

Each row is a check, each tile 1 Mb; colour is the ALT share of its reads at the run’s sites. A block of high share on one chromosome is donor DNA in that region (a mislabel or an introgressed segment); an even haze over the genome is leakage or error.

Whose alleles

For each site where a check has ALT reads: how many of the run’s donors carry that ALT in their donor alleles. An ALT from cross-talk or contamination matches the donors of the sample it came from; a sequencing error matches whatever donors share the site by chance.

ALT reads at sites where a single donor carries the ALT, by that donor’s taxon.
